title: Burnt Ends
subtitle: Twice-cooked brisket point cubes in BBQ sauce
excerpt: Burnt ends are cubes of brisket point cooked twice: once low and slow until tender, then tossed in BBQ sauce and returned to a high oven until sticky and caramelised at the edges. They're intensely flavoured, slightly crisp on the outside, and meltingly soft inside.
sourceNotes: Burnt ends originated in Kansas City as the trimmed and re-cooked tips of smoked brisket, sold cheaply from the cutting board. They evolved into a dedicated BBQ item from the 1970s onwards.

recipe.yieldDescription: serves 6 as a main or 8 as a starter
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in sauce. Reheat in a covered dish at 160°C for 25 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the first low-and-slow phase a day ahead and refrigerate. Cube and do the second cook when ready to serve.

content.text: Burnt ends are the fatty, flavoursome point of the brisket cooked twice: once low and slow until the collagen has dissolved, then cubed, tossed in sauce, and returned to a high oven until sticky and slightly charred at the edges. The outside catches and caramelises while the inside stays soft. They're a meal in themselves, served in a bowl with bread on the side.

Burnt ends traditionally use the point cut of brisket, which is fattier and has a looser grain than the flat. Some supermarkets only sell the flat, which works but gives a slightly drier result. If you can only find flat-cut brisket, reduce the second cook time by 10 minutes to prevent drying out.

items.prepNote: point cut if available, or flat cut

content.text: Heat the oven to 135°C (fan 115°C / gas mark 1). Mix together the rub ingredients: {{paprika-smoked}}, {{sea-salt-flakes}}, {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{garlic-powder}}, and {{black-pepper}}. Pat the {{beef-brisket}} dry and coat all over with the rub.

Place in a lidded casserole dish. Pour {{stock-beef}} around the base. Cover and cook for four to five hours until the internal temperature reads 90 to 93°C and the meat is completely tender when pressed with a finger. Remove and rest for 15 minutes.
Make the sauce and cube the meat
Increase the oven to 220°C (fan 200°C / gas mark 7). Cut the rested brisket into 3 to 4 cm cubes, discarding any very large pieces of solid fat.

Combine {{ketchup}}, {{molasses}}, {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{cider-vinegar}}, {{worcestershire-sauce}}, and {{unsalted-butter}} in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the butter melts. Cook until the sauce is smooth and slightly thick, about five minutes.
Toss the brisket cubes in the sauce in a large roasting tray, coating every piece. Spread them out in a single layer.

Cook at 220°C for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once halfway through, until the sauce has caramelised and the edges of each cube are dark and sticky. Watch the last five minutes: the sauce can burn quickly at this temperature.

items.symptom: The cubes dry out during the second cook
items.cause: Overcooked during the first phase, or cubes cut too small.
items.fix: Cut the brisket into larger cubes (at least 3 cm) and reduce the second cook time to 15 minutes. The first cook temperature needs to be really low: check with an oven thermometer.

items.symptom: The sauce burns and sticks to the tray
items.cause: Too high a temperature, or the cubes were too close together.
items.fix: Spread the cubes with space between them and line the tray with baking paper. Keep the oven at 220°C, not higher.

items.symptom: The inside is tough and chewy even though it looks done
items.cause: The first cook didn't reach 90°C internally.
items.fix: The first cook is where the work happens. Check with a probe: the brisket must reach at least 90°C throughout. Return to the oven if needed.

items.symptom: The sauce isn't caramelising and glazing the cubes
items.cause: Too much liquid in the tray, or sauce too thin.
items.fix: Simmer the sauce a little longer before tossing. If there's excess liquid pooling in the tray, spoon it off after the first 10 minutes of the second cook.

content.text: Burnt ends started as the byproduct of slicing brisket: the charred tips and end pieces that didn't slice cleanly were thrown in a bin at the carving station, and Kansas City barbecue customers began asking for them. By the 1980s they had become a deliberate menu item, and by the 2000s the point cut was being cooked specifically to make them rather than trimmed off a flat. Serve in a bowl with bread, pickles, and a cold beer.
